{{short description|Geometry theorem relating the line segments created by intersecting chords in a circle}}
[[File:Chord theorem.svg|thumb|upright=1.0|<math>|AS|\cdot|SC|=|BS|\cdot|SD|</math>]]

In [[Euclidean geometry]], the '''intersecting chords theorem''', or just the '''chord theorem''', is a statement that describes a relation of the four [[line segment]]s created by two intersecting [[Chord (geometry)|chords]] within a [[circle]]. 
It states that the [[Product (mathematics)|product]]s of the lengths of the line segments on each chord are equal. 
It is Proposition 35 of Book 3 of [[Euclid]]'s [[Euclid's Elements|''Elements'']]. 

For example, for two chords {{mvar|AC}} and {{mvar|BD}} intersecting at point {{mvar|S}}, the following equation holds:
<math display=block>|AS|\cdot|SC|=|BS|\cdot|SD|</math>

== Proof ==

The theorem can be proven by [[similar triangles|triangle similarity]] and the [[inscribed angle theorem]].

[[File:Chord theorem proof.svg|thumb|upright=1.0|{{center|<math>\triangle ASD \sim \triangle BSC</math>}}]]

By the inscribed angle theorem, {{tmath|1= \angle BCA=\angle ADB}} and {{tmath|1= \angle  DAC=\angle CBD}}, as each pair [[subtended angle|intercepts]] a common chord. [[Opposite angle]]s at the point {{tmath|S}} are also congruent, {{tmath|1= \angle ASD=\angle BSC}}. Therefore {{tmath|\triangle ASD}} and {{tmath|\triangle BSC}} are similar triangles, with congruent corresponding angles.

The sides of one triangle are uniformly proportional to the corresponding sides of any similar triangle, so
<math display=block>\frac{|AS|}{|BS|}=\frac{|SD|}{|SC|},</math>
or, equivalently,
<math display=block>|AS|\cdot|SC|=|BS|\cdot|SD|.</math>

== Related concepts ==

The converse is true as well. That is: If for two line segments {{mvar|{{overline|AC}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|BD}}}} intersecting in {{mvar|S}} the [[equation]] above holds true, then their four endpoints {{math|''A'', ''B'', ''C'', ''D''}} lie on a common circle. Or in other words, if the [[diagonal]]s of a [[quadrilateral]] {{mvar|ABCD}} intersect in {{mvar|S}} and fulfill the equation above, then it is a [[cyclic quadrilateral]].

[[File:Chord theorem power.svg|thumb|upright=1.0|
<math>\begin{align}
& |AS|\cdot|SC| = |BS|\cdot|SD| \\ 
={}& (r+d)\cdot(r-d) = r^2-d^2
\end{align}</math>]]

By applying the '''chord theorem''' to a third chord (a diameter) going through the circle's center {{mvar|M}} and point {{mvar|S}}, the following relationships can be made:
<math display=block>|AS|\cdot|SC| = |BS|\cdot|SD| = r^2-d^2,</math>
where {{mvar|r}} is the [[radius]] of the circle and {{mvar|d}} is the distance between the circle's center {{mvar|M}} and point {{mvar|S}}.

Next to the [[tangent-secant theorem]] and the [[intersecting secants theorem]], the intersecting chords theorem represents one of the three basic cases of a more general theorem about two intersecting lines and a circle: the [[Power_of_a_point#Theorems|power of a point]] theorem. The distance {{mvar|d}} from the circle's center {{mvar|M}} to the [[Line–line intersection|intersection point]] {{mvar|S}} is the [[absolute value]] of the power of {{mvar|S}} with respect to the circle.
